abstract: Rapid terrain-aware locomotion training must accelerate experience collection without sacrificing coherent trajectories. Keeping simulation, data collection, and proximal policy optimization (PPO) on one GPU reduces CPU-GPU transfers. Because the shared mesh cannot readily change at resets, an adaptive curriculum relocates robots among tiled terrains, advancing successful robots and lowering difficulty after insufficient progress without regenerating terrain. Large minibatches and time-out bootstrapping adapt PPO to this setting, but adequate per-robot rollout lengths constrain useful parallelism. The policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights; friction randomization, observation noise, pushes, and actuator modeling prepare it for transfer. With 4,096 ANYmal C robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 updates, training took under 20 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation. In simulation, stair crossings without base contact achieved nearly 100% success for steps up to 0.2 m, but obstacle success declined with difficulty and uphill traversal failed beyond 25 degrees. The fixed policy negotiated stairs and obstacles on physical ANYmal C, establishing hardware deployment under this setup, although imperfect lidar-derived terrain maps reduced robustness and prompted limiting velocity commands to 0.6 m/s.
methods: Proximal policy optimization (PPO) uses a critic to estimate an infinite-horizon sum of discounted future rewards, but resets can truncate that return. Failures and goal completion are predictable task endings. Time limits are different: episode time is absent from observations, so the critic cannot anticipate when an otherwise continuing trajectory will be interrupted. Treating that interruption as terminal would discard its predicted future return. The modified environment interface therefore reports time-outs separately, and the reward at a time-out is augmented with the critic's discounted estimate of the remaining return. The critic target thus includes continuation value rather than treating the reset as task completion. Episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short rollout batches, so time-outs can occur within a batch, not just at its final step. A policy update does not itself reset the environments.
results: Figure 4 shows a task-specific compromise between episode reward and training time, not a monotonic learning benefit from more robots. The simplified task reduces maximum stair and obstacle heights and removes the curriculum so improving policies are not assigned harder terrain. Rewards are reported as means and standard deviations over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, increasing robot count shortens each robot's rollout and training time, but reward drops sharply at excessive counts. The authors link this decline to insufficient temporal information for generalized advantage estimation; throughput gains also slow beyond roughly 4,000 robots. With fewer robots, reward decreases gradually, which the authors suggest reflects less diverse, correlated samples. Larger batches improve reward and postpone the decline but take longer to train. The 20,000-robot, million-sample baseline yields the highest reported reward at greater training cost, not under a matched batch budget. About 2,048-4,096 robots with roughly 100,000-200,000 samples per batch offer the reported balance for this task, reflecting temporal-data requirements and slowing throughput gains.
notes: Retained the joint GPU/curriculum contribution by linking reduced transfers to parallel collection and terrain relocation to difficulty progression. Figure 4 evaluates parallelism without curriculum, not the curriculum's isolated benefit. Figure 4's exact reward values, training times, and standard deviations are unavailable in the supplied text; no hardware success rate is reported. The selected batch implies 24 steps per robot despite reported difficulty below 25; both are retained without numerical repair or a universal threshold. Additional robot policies were retrained, with A1 and Cassie requiring changes. Teacher-student integration remains future work.
